articles.fullContent: In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it? Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing. So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working. It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask. So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone??? This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp[1], but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet! Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra. Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements.

articles.contentSnippet:

articles.fullContent: Okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI. When you are working on a problem that has endless possibilities, it is difficult to constrain yourself to a limited set of features. Can I just add one more? I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables. I have been using it to help find heisenbugs, to make profile-guided optimization reproducible, and to make Nix builds bit-reproducible. But the most fun has been using it to understand performance. Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines. I have been using it to analyze the critical path of builds. What is the critical path? The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in a program. It is the minimum time that the program can take to complete, regardless of how many resources you throw at it. The only way to make a program faster is to shorten the critical path. A B C D waits E ← critical path extra CPUs run B, C and D concurrently; A → C → E still sets the minimum runtime If you worship at the altar of Brendan Gregg, you know he spent years turning performance analysis from a dark art into a science. This is a small offering to him. 🤲 I added a new rewind time command to Rewind that analyzes a recording and tells you where the time went and what would make the run finish sooner. You can drill into any part of that answer and see the source lines responsible for it. It’s like Brendan Gregg’s flame graphs but on steroids for the critical path and with a debugger attached.11All the ideas for the command are either inspired by or directly influenced by Brendan Gregg’s work. Kneel before Zod! Aside: New to Rewind? Start with a flaky build you only catch once and dafuq is a deterministic VM? Let’s see how it works by analyzing the critical path of a libuv build and test run. The build and test suite takes 78 seconds inside Rewind, and even with 64 cores it still takes 47 seconds. Why? The usual answer is to look at a CPU profile, and in this case a CPU profile would be almost useless. For two thirds of those 47 seconds, the work the build is waiting on is not computing at all: it is asleep. 💤💤💤 §Where the time goes Every rewind time starts with two numbers: $ rewind time 7a29e716 libuv-1.51.0 78.0 s elapsed on the VM's one CPU 47.4 s critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs 67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing The first is how long the run took on the VM’s one virtual CPU. The second is the critical path: the longest chain of work where each step had to wait for the one before. No number of CPUs makes a run shorter than its critical path, so the gap between the two numbers is all that parallelism can buy you. The line under the two numbers applies Gregg’s thread state analysis. Here the biggest state is asleep: 23 seconds in epoll_pwait and 8.5 in clock_nanosleep. A sleeping thread is invisible to a CPU profiler. Gregg’s answer is off-CPU analysis: look at where threads block, not only where they compute. On a live machine, off-CPU analysis is hard. Linux can trace which thread woke which, and Gregg built wakeup and off-wake profiling on top of that, but you have to be tracing before the slow run happens, the tracing has a cost, and most of the sleeps you capture are noise. Rewind already logs every context switch because it needs them to replay, and now it records every wakeup and who caused it too. All that juicy information is in every recording. 🤤 Here is the whole output for libuv: $ rewind time 7a29e716 libuv-1.51.0 78.0 s elapsed on the VM's one CPU 47.4 s critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs 67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing The critical path by phase 3.54 s configurePhase ██ 1.67 s buildPhase █ 42.0 s checkPhase █████████████████████ 99 ms 5 other phases The critical path by process on path pid process, with what it started 47.4 s 3

articles.fullContent: I'm an independent security researcher. Over the years I've reported vulnerabilities to a number of vendors and manufacturers, and several of those reports have become CVEs. For most of the past year I've been working on Google's current Pixel phones. I reverse engineered the Samsung radio stack (under embargo), the IMS and RTP media code, the Trusty trusted apps, the MediaTek M90 modem RIL and the Android telephony framework, amongst other things. In that time I filed 95 reports through the Android and Google Devices Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP), and around 95% of them came with a working proof of concept. In total, the VRP has paid me $250, in a single payment. I should say at the outset that I have nothing against Google. My project Box began as a fork of their AI Edge Gallery; I've worked on it most days for a year, and Google have taken features from my fork back into their own. I also maintain Iris, a hardened fork of Chromium. Much of what I do is built on Google's work. This page is solely about what happened to the security bugs I reported through their programme over twelve months. Three things kept happening. Bugs were fixed after being closed. For every closed report, I extracted the relevant binary from Google's current factory image and compared the exact function the report referred to. Eight had been fixed in shipped code, with a bounds check, a permission or a validation step added precisely where I'd said one was missing. All eight had originally been closed as a "duplicate" or as "not a vulnerability". None was paid and none was credited. Two more have since been fixed in the QPR3 beta. Bugs were closed for reasons the code doesn't bear out. More than a dozen others were closed as duplicate, infeasible or "can't reproduce", yet the defect is still there, unchanged, in the current build. I'm not suggesting anyone owes a reward for a bug that hasn't been fixed, and I'm not claiming one. My point is simply that the stated reasons for closing them don't hold up once you look at the binary. A reward promised in writing has never been paid. In January Google confirmed a valid bug and raised both its severity and its reward, in writing. Three months later they reversed all of it, with no new evidence. They then said they would "stand by our word" and pay $250 anyway as a "discretionary payment exception". That was in January. Ten months of "processing", "soon" and "no date" later, it still hasn't been paid. The report itself was submitted before December 2025. One line in that thread still puzzles me. Google told me in writing that they were paying the Safety Center reward "even though our final technical assessment rated it as a duplicate of a report with no security impact." If the bug had no security impact, there is nothing to pay for. If it's worth paying for, then it did have an impact. Both statements are in the same ticket. Where things stand $250 Safety Center reward (Moderate). Approved in writing in January and confirmed in writing several times since. Ten months on it remains unpaid, and the ticket has been closed. Two High severity reports, still "Assigned". Google formally rated both as High. Neither has a reward decision or a CVE yet. One of them has already been fixed in shipped code three times: in the QPR3 beta (DP11.261002.005) in October, in the public November stable release (CP4A.261105.040.D1, rolled out to all Pixels on 10 November 2026), and again in the latest QPR3 beta (DP11.261030.003, released on 12 November 2026). The ticket is still "Assigned" and the reward field is still empty. One Moderate report, still "Assigned". Rated Moderate on 28 October. No reward decision. Ten findings fixed after being closed. Each was closed as a duplicate, infeasible or not a vulnerability, and later fixed in shipped code. No reward and no credit for any of them. Total received: $250. articles.fullContent: I own an old, cheap TV. It has no Internet connection, no fancy smart features that make you want to install a Pi-hole, and no ask-me-again-later updates. Quite basic, but it does its job well However, it is connected to my own desktop computer through an HDMI cable, so I can watch movies and TV series from the couch. Setting it up used to involve going to my desk, enabling the secondary monitor, opening the relevant application, moving its window to the secondary monitor, setting it in fullscreen, going back to the couch, remembering I forgot my wireless keyboard, getting off the couch, grabbing my wireless keyboard, going back to the couch again, and then pressing the Space bar. The most important quality of a programmer is laziness. So, of course, I vowed never to get off the couch unnecessarily. And that meant controlling everything from the TV remote. My TV remote: for some reason, the TV came with a universal remote of a different brand So, I got myself an IR transmitter and an IR receiver to tinker with: Then, I fished out an ESP32-C3 Mini devboard, a mini-breadboard, and a handful of jumper wires, and made the most basic device that could solve my woes: The great thing about Espressif MCUs is the integrated Wi-Fi radio, which makes it trivial to make devices that you connect to your Wi-Fi network. I have played around with Espressif MCUs before, including for early versions of the OmniMorse, but I must admit that Claude is just faster at it than I am. With the help of Opus 5.5, I identified the RC-5 IR codes for each remote button, and set up a few scripts so that a single button press on the remote would do the whole dance I described above. Problem solved! But this first success unlocked much more. I also own a bunch of old consoles. Getting everything hooked up is a chore, and makes a mess of wires. It would be much simpler to run an emulator on my computer and show it on the TV. Not mine, but this gives you an idea. Thus, I installed DuckStation, PCSX2, Dolphin, Cemu and ES-DE, configured two Xbox controllers on each of them, and got Claude to start everything from a single button on the remote. At this point, I was using two of the four colored buttons of the TV remote. So, of course, I had to come up with two more modes. I got Claude to add a Fireplace mode, which just plays 10-hour videos, the most important one being a fireplace. And also Steam, in Big Picture mode. Soon, there were regular issues with windows opening on the wrong screen, so I switched approaches. Instead of a large desktop on two screens, I resorted to multiseat, which I had always wanted to use, with two separate X sessions, one on each screen. This also allows using both screens at the same time without interference. But that did mean I could not directly control the windows on the TV from my regular session. So, again, I got Claude to make me an admin panel: The virtual TV remote actually works, by sending directly through the device I cobbled together. The device also tracks volume being changed from the real remote, so things stay in sync. The rest is just commands to my computer, including a virtual gamepad, and a real-time stream of what is being displayed (mouse clicks work too!). Also, turning on an Xbox controller switches to the emulator or Steam mode, and turning the last one off goes back to the fireplace. Last, but not least, I took a significant amount of time making (telling Claude to make) everything fast. The whole thing took me about 10 hours in total, most of which was setting up console emulators. Claude still needs to be kept on a tight leash: it sometimes wanted to go in the wrong direction, left obvious bugs, or suggested fixes that did not address the root cause. However, it saved me a bunch of time on the original problem, and lowered the effort enough to go above and beyond!

articles.fullContent: Governor Kathy Hochul today signed a bill restricting motor vehicle manufacturers and dealers from charging consumers subscription fees after they purchase a vehicle. Amid rising consumer prices, the new law guards against a rising trend of car companies charging car owners fees to activate and use built-in features like heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.“New Yorkers are already struggling with rising prices due to Trump’s affordability crisis, and we’re not going to let harmful business practices increase the cost of living even more,” Governor Hochul said. “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. articles.fullContent: Nov 23, 2026 - 13 min read For more than twenty years, “the mail server” in most companies meant Microsoft Exchange, and “the mail client” meant Outlook. Today we are releasing Stalwart 1.2.0, and with it Stalwart becomes a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange. Stalwart now implements the protocols that Exchange clients speak: MAPI over HTTP, Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover. Outlook, Apple Mail and the mail apps on phones and tablets connect to Stalwart as they would to an Exchange server, with mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes in one account. Users type their email address and password, Autodiscover does the rest, and they keep working in the client they already know. Exchange support is part of the open source Community edition, under the AGPL. Exchange on premises in 2026Section titled “Exchange on premises in 2026” Before going into what Stalwart now does, it is worth looking at where self-hosted Exchange stands today, because it explains why so many organisations are looking for a way out. Microsoft has not announced the end of Exchange Server. On paper, on-premises Exchange still exists. In practice, every road Microsoft is building leads to Exchange Online: Exchange 2016 and 2019 are out of support. Both reached end of support on 14 October 2025. Microsoft sold a paid Extended Security Update programme for a while, and according to press reports of an Exchange team statement, it ended in October 2026 with no further extension. Servers still running those versions receive no fixes of any kind. No new features. Exchange Server Subscription Edition (SE) is now the only supported on-premises Exchange, and there will be no more major versions after it. SE does not receive the features developed for the cloud. Even its first cumulative update has slipped from late 2025 to an undetermined date in 2026. The new Outlook does not support it. Microsoft’s own documentation for the new Outlook for Windows says it plainly: “On-premises Exchange accounts aren’t supported.” The APIs are moving to the cloud. New functionality ships only on Microsoft Graph, a cloud API. Exchange Web Services in Exchange Online started being switched off in October 2026 and will be gone entirely in April 2027. None of these steps forces anyone to move on its own. Together, they leave an Exchange administrator with a shrinking set of choices: keep running a server that will not grow, or move the organisation’s mail into Microsoft’s cloud. For many organisations the second option is not acceptable. Email is the record of a company’s contracts, negotiations, legal advice, HR matters and customer data. Placing it with a US provider means placing it within reach of US law, including the CLOUD Act, which allows US authorities to compel American providers to hand over data they control wherever it is stored. Public administrations, healthcare providers, law firms, defence contractors and many European companies cannot accept that, or no longer want to. Data sovereignty means that you decide where your data lives, under which jurisdiction, and who can read it. A mail service in someone else’s cloud cannot offer that, and an on-premises server whose vendor is steering its customers toward that cloud offers less of it every year. Outlook without ExchangeSection titled “Outlook without Exchange” The obstacle to leaving Exchange has rarely been the server. It has been the client. Many people have spent their whole working life in Outlook. They have years of muscle memory in it: their folder layout, their rules, their calendar views, their shared mailboxes, the way they book meeting rooms. Many organisations also have workflows built around it, such as delegated calendars managed by an assistant. articles.title: Show HN: Costcatch – A CLI tool for Agent cost tracking and Debugging
articles.contentSnippet:
Costcatch is CLI tool that helps you trace and debug AI agent loops and lets you see what your agent did and what it cost.
It gives a step-by-step trace of your AI agent's calls, errors, tokens, and spend - right in your terminal.
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50627927
Points: 1
# Comments: 0
articles.fullContent: See what your AI agent did, what it cost, and where it went wrong. Put costcatch in front of the command that runs your agent.Nothing to add to your code, nothing to sign up for, and nothing leaves your machine. costcatch python my_agent.py Contents Why costcatch Install Quick start Trace a whole app How it works What you see What it catches Commands Use it in CI Supported providers What is exact and what is estimated Your data Privacy and security Configuration Troubleshooting Limitations Contributing An AI agent is a loop. Every turn it sends the whole conversation to a model, runs the tools the model asks for, adds their results, and goes again. Both the cost and the bugs hide in that loop: Costs add up quietly. The history is sent again on every turn, so one big tool result is paid for on every call after it. A silent retry, or an agent stuck repeating itself, multiplies the bill. Failures hide. The SDK retries a rate limit without telling you. A tool fails and the model works around it. An answer gets cut off at max_tokens. The run still "finishes", and all you see is the final answer. Your provider's dashboard can't help. It shows a daily total per model. It can't tell you which step of which run, which tool, or why. Most tracing tools need setup first. You wrap your client in their SDK, send your traffic through their proxy, or upload your prompts to their cloud. costcatch runs your agent and records every LLM API call it makes, from outside your code. While the agent runs, each call shows up live in your terminal. When it ends, you get the whole run step by step: the model, tokens and cost of each call, the tools the model asked for and how big their results were, what failed and why, and warnings that point at what to fix. Question Where costcatch answers it Which step failed, and why? ✗ rows with the HTTP status and the provider's message, and failed tools with their error Which step costs the most? The cost of every step, with a bar, and a warning when one step costs more than the rest together Which tool result is bloating every prompt? The size of every tool result, and a warning for big results sent again and again Did the agent loop, retry, or get cut off? Loop, retry, duplicate and cut-off warnings Where did the time go? Time in LLM calls against time in your own code and tools Did my change make it worse? diff, --compare-last, and CI gates on cost, calls and errors How it compares: Approach Examples What it asks of you SDK-based tracing LangSmith, Langfuse, Braintrust Add their SDK to your code and send traces to their server Proxies and gateways Helicone, LiteLLM Proxy Point your API base URL at the proxy OpenTelemetry OpenLLMetry, APM vendors Add instrumentation and run a collector costcatch Put costcatch in front of your command costcatch is a tool for the machine you're developing on. It isn't production monitoring, and it works fine next to any of the tools above. Install The published npm package, v0.2.0, requires Node.js 20.19 or later. To trace Python agents you also need Python 3.8 or later; there's nothing to pip install. npm install -g costcatch costcatch init # once: downloads current prices for every model Or run it without installing: npx costcatch python my_agent.py. To build it from source: git clone https://github.com/RonakRahane/costcatch.git cd costcatch npm ci npm run build npm link # puts the costcatch command on your PATH Quick start costcatch init # first, once: download current prices for every model costcatch python my_agent.py # trace a Python agent costcatch node my_agent.js # trace a Node.js agent Run costcatch init before your first trace, and again now and then to pick up new prices. Without it, costcatch only knows a small bundled price list, so newer models show $?.??, and costcatch reminds you to run it. The init screen This is the full terminal screen from costcatch init. articles.fullContent: allume-web-export turns an Allume board export into a static website: a page for every board, which visitors can pan, zoom and move between as they would in Allume. Allume (formerly Muse) is a spatial canvas for thinking and organizing ideas. This tool lets you publish those boards on the open web, either as a standalone website or embedded in an existing site. See it in action: Fragments & Flows, a digital garden that uses the exporter. For the motivation behind the project, read Opening the Pensieve: Web Exporting for Allume. Demos Deployed as a standalone website in Programming. Embedded within the Fragments & Flows digital garden. Install The tool runs on macOS 14 or later. With Homebrew brew install oktana-coop/tap/allume-web-export From a Release Each release has the tool as a zip: the command and its resource bundle, which the command needs beside it. From Source With Xcode 26 or later, build the tool from this repository: The command is then .build/release/allume-web-export. Usage Run In Allume, export the board to publish with Export Board As › Allume Bundle…. The boards inside it are exported with it, into a zip archive named after the board, such as Programming.muse. Run the tool on the bundle, with one of its two commands, which publish the boards in two ways: site as a website of their own, and embed for an existing site to show in its own pages. Either way, PDFs are never published: their cards show only their title. A folder decompressed from the bundle, with contents.json, metadata.json and files/ in it, works too. Site allume-web-export site path/to/bundle.muse --out site The site's folder then holds: index.html, the exported board's page; a page for every board inside it, named after its label with a short code, such as functional-q5tbqj.html; files/, with the images, handwriting, avatars and favicons the pages show. Images in a format browsers can't show, such as HEIC, are published as JPEG instead, or as PNG when they have transparent pixels. In previews/, it has the previews board cards show: each board as a first visit opens it, from its top left at 100% in a window 1440 px wide, its own board cards showing their previews, scaled down to the card. They're images in the light and dark palettes, such as <board-id>-light.jpg, and for a colored card on its color, such as <board-id>-purple-light.jpg. WebKit draws them, and when it can't, the board's cards show an empty panel, with a warning; allume.css and allume.js, the viewer. Embed allume-web-export embed path/to/bundle.muse --out allume Its folder holds: boards.json, which lists the boards, each with its label, a suggested slug, the boards it's on and its view's path, and gives the preview images' paths; boards/, each board's view, an element for a page to include, whose links and images are allume: references for the site to replace with its own URLs, as References explains; preview-light.jpg and preview-dark.jpg, pictures of the whole exported board, 1600 px wide, in the light and dark palettes. WebKit draws them, and when it can't, they're left out with a warning; files/, as for a site; allume.css and allume.js, the viewer, for the site's pages to include. To have the views link to the site's URLs instead, give embed the site's patterns: each board's URL, with {slug} standing for its slug, and where the site serves the folder's files/: allume-web-export embed path/to/bundle.muse --out allume --board-url '/boards/{slug}/' \ --files-url /allume/files Either can be given alone, leaving the other kind of reference in. articles.fullContent: Postvec is an extension for fused hybrid search: it combines BM25 and semantic search in one SQL call and keeps vectors in sync with your text automatically. You can also use it to migrate vectors without re-embedding of text with direct conversion between embedding formats. Inference runs locally inside PostgreSQL or remote on postvec-server or through hosted embedding APIs. docker run -d --name postvec -p 5432:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postvec \ ghcr.io/univec-ai/postvec:pg18-local Wait until docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' postvec prints healthy. Then: CREATE TABLE docs (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, body text); SELECT postvec.enable( 'public.docs', 'body', model => 'sentence-transformers-all-minilm-l6-v2' ); INSERT INTO docs (body) VALUES ('quarterly revenue guidance was raised'), ('embedding model migration without source re-embedding'); -- vectors fill after commit; wait until postvec.status() shows pending_jobs = 0 SELECT d.*, s.rrf_score FROM postvec.search('public.docs', 'body', 'switching vector models') AS s JOIN docs AS d ON d.id = s.pk_value::bigint ORDER BY s.rrf_score DESC; To change the stored model: SELECT postvec.migrate('public.docs', 'body', 'baai-bge-m3'); Old rows convert through an embedding-space translator. New writes use the new model. The columns swap at migration_finalize(). Install Host Start here Try it Quick start (one container) or quick start remote Existing PostgreSQL 16, 17 or 18 Packages, then postvec setup RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, Azure, Supabase, Neon Managed PostgreSQL Downloads: postvec.dev/download. Docs: postvec.dev/docs. Inference Embedded (postvec.mode = 'embedded', default). The engine runs in the PostgreSQL process. Models live on local disk. The local image includes MiniLM (384-d). Remote (postvec.mode = 'grpc'). PostgreSQL sends work to postvec-server: GPU, process isolation, a fleet, or a host that cannot load a third-party .so. SQL is the same. Hosted embedding APIs (OpenAI, Cohere, Bedrock, Gemini, Mistral, OpenRouter, UniVec) are optional per column. Keys live in 0600 files on the inference host. Providers. License The extension, CLI, engine, providers and packaging use the PostgreSQL License. postvec-server uses Business Source License 1.1 (source-available). Development, testing, personal production and one 30-day production evaluation per organization are free. Organizational production use needs postvec Pro. Each version converts to the PostgreSQL License four years after release. LICENSING.md. Source cargo build --workspace # CLI, server, engine cd postvec && cargo pgrx test pg18 # extension tests cd postvec && ./ci.sh # full local gate Needs Rust, cargo-pgrx 0.18.1, a pgrx-managed PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector, and protoc. Render the prompt template with strongly-typed input const prompt = prompts.decodeCatMood.render({ catAction: "Sit on keyboard", bowlStatus: "half-empty", }); // 2. articles.title: Figma employee sues, alleging company forced her to confront harassers
articles.contentSnippet: Figma and its CEO are being sued by a current employee for alleged sexual harassment and discrimination.
articles.fullContent: A Figma engineer is suing the design software company and its co-founder and CEO, Dylan Field, over allegations that she faced sexual harassment and retaliation while managers and HR repeatedly told her to confront the very people she accused of misconduct. The lawsuit, filed Monday in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, alleges that Figma’s culture of “direct feedback” led managers and HR to make engineer Serry Park address harassment herself rather than investigate her complaints. Park, who joined Figma in 2022, alleges the company’s response damaged her career, compensation, and mental health. The lawsuit also alleges that Park, who is Asian, faced racial and gender discrimination, including performance criticism based on stereotypes that Asian women are meek, timid, and conflict-averse. “Figma was my dream company for a long time,” Park told TechCrunch in an interview before the lawsuit was filed. “It was a place where I felt that I could level up in my career, working on a lot of really cool, interesting things at scale.” Park is seeking damages, a jury trial, and a court order prohibiting Figma from requiring employees who report harassment to confront their alleged harassers. She also wants the company to adopt and enforce a process for investigating harassment complaints promptly and confidentially. When reached for comment, a spokesperson for Figma said, “Figma does not tolerate discrimination or harassment. Figma also does not tolerate extortion. These claims have no merit, and we will present the facts in court.” Faith in the Process Park told TechCrunch she initially had faith in Figma’s complaint process, expecting that if she documented the alleged harassment and reported it to the right people, the company would act. But as an engineer in a male-dominated field, Park told TechCrunch, “I don’t feel that they took me seriously throughout this process.” Park, who is still employed at Figma, joined its San Francisco office in October 2022. Within weeks, her onboarding mentor — a fellow engineer — asked her on a date and continued pursuing her after she declined, Park alleges. She initially feared reporting him, worrying that her manager would “dismiss her reports or view her as the problem,” according to the lawsuit. Park says she tried to avoid her onboarding mentor. In early 2023, for example, she delayed choosing a work project until he had picked one. When her manager criticized her for not being a “team player,” Park explained that she was trying to avoid the colleague she accused of harassment, according to the suit. Her manager allegedly dismissed her concerns, saying he had “met his wife at work too” and treating the behavior as “harmless flirtation.” When Park asked to be kept off projects with the onboarding mentor, HR allegedly instructed her to confront him directly about his behavior. The lawsuit ties that response to Figma’s culture of direct feedback, which Park alleges Field established and enforced. It says the company’s People organization trains managers to direct employees, including those reporting harassment, to give feedback directly to the person involved. In March 2023, her manager assigned him to a major project she was leading, despite her request to be separated from him. Park told her manager that she would “figure it out,” but alleges that having to work with him affected her performance. Her manager gave her a 2 out of 5 on her performance review, criticizing her for not speaking up enough or engaging with others and for lacking presence. Park was put on a coaching plan, which she completed in late 2023. Changing managers didn’t help, according to the lawsuit. articles.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes
articles.contentSnippet: As AI-generated code piles up, Anthropic's new developer tools aim to eliminate another bottleneck by letting agents handle routine approvals.
articles.fullContent: Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship, a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes. The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team. Image Credits:Anthropic The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself. “Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.” Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge. The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed. Image Credits:Anthropic Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language. Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first. Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process. Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision. Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub. Code Review is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals are in beta. articles.fullContent: AI investing startup Supertake has an interesting premise: What if your “takes” on the market could make you money without you having to pick stocks yourself? The service lets people turn their ideas into real investment portfolios, using frontier AI models and trading agents. Now, the company has raised $20 million in seed funding to grow its business. The round was led by venture firm Adjacent (Nico Wittenborn), with participation from Coinbase Ventures and Union Square Ventures (USV). Numerous angel investors also joined, including Nat Friedman, who’s currently head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs; Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch; renowned product manager Nikita Bier; investor Scott Belsky; and Nemil Dalal, a former Coinbase exec who is now a visiting partner at Y Combinator. Michael Mignano originally incubated the startup at USV. He is the co-founder and former CEO of the podcasting platform Anchor, which Spotify acquired in 2019 for over $150 million. While he will continue in his role as founder and executive chairman, he’s now brought in a team to run the company day to day. The team includes co-founders Lincoln Murr (CEO) and John Peterson (CTO). Both joined from Coinbase, where, Mignano notes, they were the heads of AI product and engineering, leading launches like Coinbase advisor, Coinbase for agents, agentic wallets, and others. The startup arrives as AI continues to make inroads into financial services, but allowing AI to take over people’s actual investments requires a new level of trust. Supertake is betting that people will ultimately be willing to take that leap, given recent improvements in frontier AI models. Currently, Supertake works with Coinbase and Robinhood, and the company intends to expand to more brokerages over time. The idea is that you can explain, in broad, natural language, what you believe about how the world is going to change, and Supertake’s AI will iterate with you back and forth to turn that idea into a “take” that’s investable. articles.title: Elon Musk and others rejoice as Jensen Huang is reinstated at Nvidia amid scandal
articles.contentSnippet: "The mistake has been corrected," Elon Musk chimed in.
articles.fullContent: A handful of tech CEOs, including Elon Musk, are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia. Despite being caught in three affairs — including one with an alleged Chinese spy that has triggered multiple congressional investigations over national security concerns — Huang was reinstated as CEO and president of Nvidia on Monday morning. “The mistake has been corrected,” Tesla and SpaceX leader Elon Musk wrote on X about Huang’s return. Musk had been among the most vocal tech leaders to advocate for Huang. “I think it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak, and it just doesn’t seem like a good thing for shareholders,” Musk said last week at the DealBook Summit. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had taken a more neutral stance, commenting last week, “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.” Altman had experienced a similar situation when he was ousted as CEO of OpenAI, then reinstated days later. After the announcement that Huang would return, Altman simply posted, “Jensen!” Many other tech CEOs have similarly refrained from commenting on the matter, given the shifting politics surrounding Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, as well as the national security concerns at the center of the controversy. articles.title: Megaspeed, the company at the center of the Jensen Huang scandal, appears headed for a US blacklist
articles.contentSnippet: Megaspeed, which was previously led by Alice Huang, would be barred from doing business with U.S. companies unless those companies attained a special license from the federal government.

This list “contains the names of foreign parties” subject to certain export restrictions designed to ensure that “sensitive technologies do not fall into the hands of those who would threaten U.S. national security or American citizens.” Functionally, what this will mean is that U.S. companies will not be able to do business with or sell products to Megaspeed without first gaining a special license from the federal government. Last week, the Commerce Department also announced it had launched a criminal probe into the company. Authorities in both the U.S. and Singapore are now probing whether the company defied export restrictions and illegally smuggled Nvidia chips to China. The company has denied wrongdoing. articles.fullContent: Google announced on Monday that it’s expanding Personal Intelligence in Search’s AI Mode with integrations for Google Drive, Google Wallet, and the Gemini app. Personal Intelligence is designed to offer users more personalized, context-aware answers by connecting to their Google apps and drawing on information from their digital lives. The feature can already connect to apps like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Photos. By bringing Personal Intelligence in AI Mode to Drive, Wallet, and the Gemini app, Google is leveraging the wealth of user data that’s already within its ecosystem. Since users rely on these services, the tech giant can deliver more personalized experiences that rivals aren’t able to match. Of course, not everyone wants AI looking at their Wallet and Drive, so connecting the apps is optional, and you can turn Personal Intelligence on or off at any time. Google says that connecting Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence lets users track their financial goals, cut everyday spending, and make better use of credit card rewards. The tech giant notes that if users choose to connect their Wallet, AI Mode can only read information from accounts and isn’t able to move or manage their money. Image Credits:Google As for Drive, the company says important information related to a project or major decision is often scattered across documents and spreadsheets. By connecting Google Drive to Personal Intelligence, AI can draw on those files to provide more relevant, personalized answers, such as creating a tailored plan for tax season. Users will also be able to share context between their Gemini app and AI Mode in Search, which means that if they explore an idea in the Gemini app, they won’t have to start over with AI Mode because it will already have the information, and vice versa. Additionally, Google says users will soon be able to view the context that AI Mode uses via a new “Personalization” icon that will appear below responses. The company also announced on Monday that users will start to see more personally relevant responses in AI Overviews and AI Mode that will be tailored to users’ recent search context. articles.fullContent: Meta’s new sustainability report buries the lead: The company is almost certain to miss its own goal to reach net zero by 2030, and it’s refusing to commit to a new timeline. “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets — so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” wrote Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net-zero and sustainability at Meta, in the introduction to the company’s 2026 sustainability report. That’s a lot of words to say that Meta will continue to pollute if that means it can continue its AI rollout. Such is the risk of voluntary targets. Companies can make and break them with little to lose, betting — often rightly — that they can ignore them with just a small hit to public opinion, which is fickle anyway. (Remember the Cambridge Analytica scandal? Most people don’t.) There’s almost no risk to the bottom line. “We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline and interim milestone. We’ll continue investing in emissions reductions and reporting our progress annually,” a Meta spokesperson told TechCrunch. A few years ago, Meta was arguably one of the better corporate stewards of the climate. The company has been one of the largest purchasers of clean power, and it set ambitious goals for water conservation. More recently, though, its multibillion-dollar bet on natural gas at its Hyperion data center in Louisiana has undone much of that progress. Natural gas may burn cleaner and more efficiently than coal, but its impact on global warming can be just as bad when the leaky infrastructure needed to burn it is factored in. Despite years of clean power procurement, Meta’s greenhouse gas emissions have more than doubled in the last four years. Between 2024 and 2025, its data center emissions increased more than 12 times, and Hyperion isn’t online yet. That commitment to natural gas led to the company’s departure from RE100, a corporate renewable energy initiative, in July. The company had been part of the group for a decade, though the two split after RE100 started requiring more rigorous reporting toward renewable energy targets. “When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned,” they added. “The reality has been far more complex. Demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected, arriving on a timeline measured in quarters rather than decades, and meeting it has meant building at a pace and scale the industry has never attempted.” That’s all true, but when put that way, it sounds like Meta has little agency in the matter. But the company’s decision to chase AI was a conscious one. You could argue that Meta has a fiduciary duty to chase after its peers, which have also dived headfirst into AI. But there’s precious little data to support the idea that AI will be a profit driver for a company like Meta, which is almost entirely consumer-focused. CEO Mark Zuckerberg is optimistic that improving Muse’s energy efficiency will turn that around, but how much will everyday people be willing to pay for software that translates your offhand thoughts into surreal memes? Or monitors your emails so you won’t forget to reply to your mom? Meta is betting that it’ll be enough to support a $200 billion-plus data center, and probably more. The choice of the fuel to power those AI ambitions was also a conscious one. Natural gas power plants, besides being able to run 24/7, are actually not a great fit for AI data centers. articles.title: Jensen Huang isn’t out of the woods yet
articles.contentSnippet: Tech leaders should be clear-eyed about all the problems likely to come with Huang's reinstatement.
articles.fullContent: It’s safe to say no one expected this. Monday morning, Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia, after resigning the position following news of multiple affairs, including one with a subordinate and one with a woman tied to Chinese intelligence services. With so much of the AI industry built on top of Nvidia’s AI infrastructure, Huang’s departure looked like an imminent threat to the business — and the mood on his return has been ecstatic. Share prices are rocketing back up, particularly for neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, and the Nasdaq rose 7% on the news. Still, tech leaders should be clear-eyed about all the problems likely to come with Huang’s reinstatement. President Trump is already telling reporters that the U.S. government found no national security concerns resulting from the affair, but the broader national security concerns aren’t so easy to dismiss, and Trump’s involvement may do more harm than good for Nvidia and its partners. This isn’t the end of the problems caused by Huang’s affairs; it’s likely just the beginning. Most importantly, serious questions remain about how Nvidia chips were smuggled into China, and how much Nvidia knew about it. Among Jensen Huang’s defenders, it’s become common to question whether Alice Huang was really a spy, but it’s clear that a lot of restricted chips were flowing into China through her company. Just this weekend, The New York Times reported sustained contact between Alice Huang and a member of China’s Ministry of State Security during the same period she was having an affair with Jensen Huang. With Democrats in control of Congress, including investigative bodies like the House Oversight Committee, there are plenty of ways to force the issue. Nvidia’s role in violating U.S. export controls would likely have been the subject of prolonged uncomfortable investigation, whether Huang returned or not. But with him back in the CEO’s seat, there will be a lot more riding on any revelations that come up — and any new revelations will damage Nvidia as a company alongside Huang himself. Then there are the questions raised by Trump’s intervention. It’s unprecedented in American history for a sitting president to intervene to clear a CEO accused of being a national security risk. Simply pressing the Department of Justice to exonerate Huang would have been a scandal, but calling the Nvidia board goes significantly further. Huang has already donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom project, so it’s easy to make the case that Trump was intervening on behalf of a donor, setting national security risks aside for his personal benefit. All of this is happening just as Democrats retake Congress, with all of its associated investigative powers. Even if they can’t fire Huang or remove Trump, there are lots of uncomfortable questions that are still unanswered. Was there any Department of Justice inquiry into whether Huang had committed a crime, or did Trump make the call on his own? Did the intelligence services make any official assessment that could be subpoenaed into the congressional record? Investigating Democrats will be particularly interested in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees export controls and retains significant financial ties to the industry through his firm, Cantor Fitzgerald. If all of this sounds exhausting, you’re getting a sense of what the next year will be like for anyone following national news. Congress will keep a steady drip of embarrassing revelations, milking as much political juice as possible out of Huang and everyone associated with him. Trump will keep lashing out, often making things worse for everyone involved. (Trump’s statement to CBS, which defends Huang in racist terms while also accusing him of treason, is an early taste.) It’s going to be ugly and sad, and the most successful tech company of the last decade will be right at the center of it. I have to assume that this was the scenario the board was concerned about when it decided to remove Huang

articles.title: Trump reportedly called into Nvidia board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return
articles.contentSnippet: "I spoke to them, let me put it that way … And I convinced them," the president told CNBC.
articles.fullContent: A close ally of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, President Donald Trump reportedly dialed into an Nvidia board meeting to push for the ousted CEO’s return, Semafor reported on Monday. Trump got his way, as Nvidia announced Huang’s reinstatement shortly afterward. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way … And I convinced them,” the president told CNBC. Huang was forced to step down from his role as CEO, which he held for 33 years, after news broke that he had affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including a direct report. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor. The president took to his social media app, Truth Social, to remark that “the United States government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security.” According to Nvidia’s press release about Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and president, the company claimed that “the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” While Trump has declared that Huang “did absolutely nothing wrong,” many government officials aren’t buying the president’s point of view. Huang is still expected to testify in closed-door conversations with three committees of the House of Representatives on December 1. He is also slated to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to testify publicly, though that hearing has not been scheduled yet. “People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it’s a threat to lose him,” Trump said to CNBC. Trump has maintained this position through the scandal, even denying that he was ever told about Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang (no relation). The New York Times reported, on the contrary, that Trump’s secretary of state and national security adviser Marco Rubio briefed him aboard Air Force One in May. Earlier this spring, Rubio also supervised the drafting of a memo that circulated among top policymakers, warning that Alice Huang was spying for China’s Ministry of State Security. articles.title: CrowdStrike to acquire Zscaler for $44 billion
articles.contentSnippet: The cybersecurity giant said that the deal to buy Zscaler, which provides zero-trust products to large enterprises, will better equip their customers to use AI agents.
articles.fullContent: In Brief Posted: 8:20 AM PST · November 23, 2026 Image Credits:Benjamin Fanjoy/Bloomberg / Getty Images Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the companies announced Monday. CrowdStrike and Zscaler said that the deal will create the “largest single addressable market” for cybersecurity, which will enable the companies to better position themselves for the AI era. Zscaler is a San Jose, California-based tech company that provides cloud cybersecurity products to about 8,000 enterprise companies. The company offers zero-trust technology, a security feature that requires employees to authenticate each and every time they access an internal system or resource. The aim is to protect against hackers from stealing credentials and using them to gain unfettered access to a company’s network. CrowdStrike, which secures the computers, laptops, phones, and other devices connected to a company’s network, said the deal will unite its endpoint protection software with Zscaler’s zero-trust platform to better defend their customers against data breaches. By combining the two products, CrowdStrike and Zscaler say that they can offer “superior protection” to their customers. In remarks on Monday, the companies said that the acquisition will help customers safely adopt AI. The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, is expected to close around this time next year. articles.title: Dutch privacy authority urges consumers not to buy ‘pervert glasses’
articles.contentSnippet: The Netherlands' data protection agency said smart wearables violate people's privacy, get information wrong, and can result in unsafe situations.
articles.fullContent: In Brief Posted: 7:29 AM PST · November 23, 2026 Image Credits:David Paul Morris/Bloomberg / Getty Images The Dutch Data Protection Authority is urging consumers not to buy AI-enabled camera glasses, warning that they compromise the privacy of nearby bystanders and risk the safety of their users. The authority, whose recent statement falls just short of an outright ban, said that use of the internet-enabled and always-on glasses to record people in public is “almost always prohibited.” Critics have dubbed these smart wearables as “pervert glasses” for their propensity to be used to video people without their permission, particularly to harass women. While some glasses have warning lights when users are recording, privacy advocates have argued that these alerts are not clear enough. Some people have even made phone apps capable of detecting nearby smart glasses wearers. The Dutch data protection authority warned that the glasses also produce wrong results and unsafe results. In one test carried out by the Dutch authority, a pair of unnamed glasses “gave dating advice to an adult who indicated that they are interested in a minor.” The glasses also incorrectly read a medicine label and claimed to have called an ambulance when it had not. The Dutch government’s advice follows a similar move by the Norwegian government, which in September said it was considering a ban on camera-enabled devices. articles.title: Trump endorses Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, says US has no evidence of wrongdoing
articles.contentSnippet: The president cited the U.S. attorney general in defending Huang's return, while urging Nvidia to continue its export-control investigation.
articles.fullContent: President Trump praised Nvidia’s decision on Monday to reinstate founder Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, saying on his social network Truth Social that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” The Nvidia board’s statement had also referred to consultations with “senior levels of the United States government” as informing its decision. It said that, based on that input, Mr. Huang’s reinstatement was deemed not a national security risk. In his comments on Monday, Trump claimed that U.S. Attorney General [Todd Blanche] had found no evidence that Mr. Huang had engaged in unlawful conduct. It’s an unusual statement for a U.S. president to make, as the attorney general typically conducts those investigations independently. Notably, Attorney General Blanche has not yet made a formal statement on the case. There’s also indication that President Trump may have been aware of the decision before the announcement by the Nvidia board. Speaking to a PBS journalist over the weekend, he said of Huang “he’s back where he should be and we see he did absolutely nothing wrong.” Asked to clarify about whether he meant Huang would be reinstated, Trump said, “I hope so, I hope so.” Huang was accused of having multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a direct report at Nvidia and another unnamed employee. However, the affair of most concern was the one with the alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation). Ms. Huang was an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, which had purchased billions in Nvidia chips over the past couple of years. This relationship had raised national security concerns about whether the CEO ties to Ms. Huang could have compromised sensitive information or facilitated China’s access to advanced U.S. AI chips, which are subject to export restrictions. Trump said last week that he believed this relationship didn’t threaten the U.S.’s national security, and instead said that no one had proven she’s a spy. “She may not be a spy,” the president said, adding that “China plays games with us, and we play games with China.” Trump’s full statement on Huang’s return, released on Monday, is below. The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. articles.title: Sierra doubles valuation to $30B within six months as demand for AI in CX takes off
articles.contentSnippet: Enterprise customer experience company Sierra, co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, said on Monday that it has raised $1.75 billion in a Series F round.
articles.fullContent: Enterprise customer experience company Sierra, co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, said on Monday that it has raised $1.75 billion in a Series F round that doubles the company’s valuation to $30 billion. The new raise comes within six months of its previous round, which valued the company at $15 billion. The new round was led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed Venture Partners, with participation from existing investors who have led previous rounds, including Benchmark, Sequoia, Greenoaks, GV, and Tiger Global. Enterprise automation is among the few areas where AI has seen rapid adoption. Sierra said that it currently serves almost 50% of Fortune 50 companies, and its clients include BNY, HSBC, Singtel, Wells Fargo, JPMorganChase, Pearson, Next, and Cox Automotive. The company late last month said its outcome-based pricing model has helped it double its run-rate revenue to $400 million within five months. That said, Sierra is working along similar lines as other customer experience players in the market, which is creating a platform to build agents and partner with model developers to provide choices to enterprises. As personal and work agents interact with enterprise systems, Sierra is also working on creating protocol definitions for agents with companies like Meta, Stripe, and Walmart. Sierra will use the fresh cash build to its technology stack to layer agents for servicing and hire more sales folks to sign and maintain enterprise contracts faster than its rivals. Startups operating in the CX space have seen multimillion-dollar rounds come their way with soaring valuations. Voice AI company ElevenLabs is now valued at $22 billion; Decagon is valued at $4.5 billion; Wonderful is valued at $5 billion; and Parloa is valued at $3 billion. Multiple other startups have scored investments of more than $100 million. During the HumanX conference in Amsterdam in September, Sierra co-founder Clay Bavor argued that despite the popular belief that AI-powered CX companies are replacing humans in contact centers, a majority of its customers are reassigning roles to existing employees. articles.title: Nvidia reverses course and brings Jensen Huang back as CEO
articles.contentSnippet: The stunning reversal was supported by senior officials in the U.S. government.
articles.fullContent: In a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board said on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, less than two weeks after he resigned following his admission of at least two extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman whom the U.S. government suspects to be a Chinese spy. The decision marks an extraordinary comeback for one of the tech industry’s most influential executives, whose abrupt departure raised questions about national security and the future of the world’s most valuable chipmaker. Notably, the U.S. government itself played a role in his return: Nvidia’s board said it consulted senior government officials before determining that Huang posed no national security risk. Nvidia shares, which had already shot up in premarket trading, opened 30% higher. Nvidia shares were priced at $159.95 a share, up 27%, at 9:51 a.m. ET. In the days since Huang resigned, President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his support for the ousted executive, who is now back at the helm of the AI chip giant. Trump said in a post on Truth Social that the board “made the correct and proper decision to return” Huang to the position, noting that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Nvidia poses any risk to national security. Trump also said the U.S. attorney general confirmed that the U.S. government doesn’t have any evidence that Huang engaged in any illegal activity. A long list of high-profile tech executives were pushing the board — in social media posts and publicly aired interviews — to bring Huang back, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Atoms founder Travis Kalanick, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan — all of whom signed a petition pushing for reinstatement. The company said the board’s unanimous decision followed a series of discussions and meetings with Huang, after which they were “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.” Just a few days ago, the board had seemed immovable in its choice to push Huang out. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey C. Jones said they didn’t intend to reinstate Huang. Nvidia had even retained executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement. Jones, along with the rest of the board, now has a different view. In a prepared statement, Jones said the board believes Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of its stockholders, employees, partners, and customers. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company,” Jones said. “We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s Chief Financial Officer.” In a statement, Huang said he was honored to return to his role as the head of the company he co-founded in 1993. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said. “I want to thank the Nvidia Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading Nvidia during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.” This story is developing... articles.fullContent: Three weeks ago, Bambu Lab introduced the state of the art in home printing tech at $2,499 — now, you can get many of its fancy new features for less than half the price.Like that bigger H3C, the new $1,149 Bambu P3C can also swap between materials on the fly, mix different colors to produce much of the rainbow, mix soft and hard materials, even mix different sizes of nozzle and different diameters of filament so you can switch between high speed and fine detail in a single print.But Bambu cut more corners than I expected to hit the lower $1,149 / £999 / €1,149 launch price today, and I think they made more of a tinkerer’s 3D printer than one suited for either beginners or pros.Some of the changes were completely expected, like its smaller 256 x 256 x 260mm print area (much like Bambu’s other P-series printers), and that it supports seven automatically swapping tools instead of nine. (Seven is still quite a lot when affordable toolchangers like the $849 Snapmaker U1 typically offer just four.)But unlike the H3C, the P3C doesn’t come fully loaded, and it doesn’t load itself. While it has slots for seven rolls of filament and up to seven independent tools (including thicker-than-usual 2.85mm filament, or pens, cutting blades, and debossing and foil transfer tools if you want it to double as a Cricut), it only comes with five 0.4mm print nozzles by default.And while five is still one more color than you’d get with an $800 Bambu P2S Combo, the 3D printer I’d buy for myself, the Bambu P3C’s automated material system (AMS) is the first Bambu has shipped without any motors to automatically load your filament.Don’t get me wrong: You can still keep five colors of filament ready to go at a moment’s notice, one more than the P2S, by keeping them loaded into the P3C’s five independent nozzles. You can also buy and fairly easily install two more printheads as well, though they cost up to $100 each.But loading those nozzles is a slow and surprisingly manual process where you have to shove a string of filament down a tube, quite a long distance by hand, after waiting for the machine to preheat each one, and it feels like a step backwards after years using the earlier motorized versions of Bambu’s AMS. Then again, the P3C doesn’t have to spend time and filament purging between colors like the P2S does.I expect many 3D printing enthusiasts will see $1,149 for the Bambu P3C as a pretty good deal, assuming they haven’t written off the company’s gadgets after Bambu’s open source snafus. Even five nozzles is enough to load all five rolls of Bambu’s “PLA Palette” cyan, magenta, yellow, black, and white (CMYKW) filaments for color mixing to produce beautiful creations like the company’s new hummingbird test print, which came out almost flawlessly on my first try.But you should know that color mixing isn’t necessarily a foolproof way to produce some colors, like the brown tree branch that’s supposed to be the hummingbird’s perch, and I’m not looking forward to manually pulling and pushing a roll of brown filament to change that. Bambu says I should probably try a feature called “mixed color sublayer” for better results, and I also suppose I could daisy-chain a normal motorized AMS to one of the P3C’s printheads, as that is a supported workflow. But that’s why I’m suggesting we’re in tinkerer territory.I asked Bambu about the decision to not include filament-loading motors in the P3C’s AMS system, and here’s part of the statement I got back from spokesperson Karlie Hou: “The AMS 3P’s design deliberately omits the auto‑loading feature as part of the effort to offer premium multi‑head performance at roughly half the price of the flagship H3C system, allowing a far broader audience — hobbyists, small studios, and educational institutions — to enjoy premium multi‑head, multi‑color printing experience.”The company says it should take around five minutes to manually reload five nozzles. “In the next [software] update, we aim to shrink the total hands‑on tim

articles.fullContent: Uber’s high-stakes robotaxi bet is officially ditching its human safety net. Nuro, Lucid, and Uber are starting fully driverless public road testing in the San Francisco Bay Area, with employee-only rides launching shortly after.First announced in July 2025, this three-way alliance represents Uber’s aggressive comeback in autonomous ride-hailing, after having abandoned its own troubled in-house efforts years ago. By pulling human safety operators from behind the wheel of Lucid Gravity SUVs, the companies say they are clearing a critical hurdle toward a public launch. That debut is now slated for early 2027, marking a slight slip from the partnership’s original late-2026 target. When it finally goes live, it will pit Uber directly against entrenched rivals like Waymo and Zoox on their home turf.Image: UberDriverless testing kicks off across four South Bay cities—Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale—before expanding across the broader Bay Area next year. To fuel this push, Lucid has delivered more than 100 upgraded Gravity SUVs, up from the 75 engineering vehicles on the road earlier this year.The automaker began building pre-production models in October to clear regulatory safety approvals, and it plans to start manufacturing the actual commercial fleet in the coming weeks. Each SUV is powered by Nuro’s Level 4 “Nuro Driver” system, pairing cameras, solid-state lidar, and radar with a roof-mounted LED “halo” that flashes a rider’s initials and pickup status.Removing the human backup comes after nearly a year of round-the-clock supervised testing in the Bay Area and Houston. Before letting the cars loose on public streets alone, Nuro put the software through grueling, high-risk edge cases on a closed track in Las Vegas to prove it could handle the unpredictable chaos of real-world driving.The robotaxis are scheduled to hit the Uber app for Bay Area riders in the first quarter of 2027, with Houston following later that year. articles.fullContent: Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.Ladybird, an independent web browser with a built-from-scratch engine, is finally available for testing. On Monday, Ladybird developer Andreas Kling announced that the browser is launching in alpha on macOS and Linux following more than four years of development.The release makes Ladybird the first browser in years to arrive with an entirely new engine. We’ve seen many engines emerge over time, but the most popular browsers use just three today: Gecko, Blink, and WebKit. While Gecko, now used in Mozilla Firefox, first appeared in Netscape 6 in 2000, Apple’s WebKit arrived in Safari in 2003 as a fork of KDE’s KHTML. A decade later, the Google-backed Chromium project forked WebKit to create Blink, which now powers Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera, and more.Ladybird is backed by a nonprofit organization with the goal of creating “an independent, fast and secure browser that respects user privacy and fosters an open web,” according to its website. Though Ladybird development initially began as part of a C++ project, its developers eventually began porting the code to Rust using AI.In his post announcing the alpha, Kling notes that the browser built around the Ladybird engine “is modest but functional,” adding that “some websites won’t work” during the alpha. A Windows version of Ladybird will arrive during a “later stage” of the project.Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.Emma Roth

Smith’s radio show shortly after the news came out, Trump said that Huang would “end up on his feet.”“You know the expression, anybody can be replaced,” Trump said, floating Apple’s ex-CEO Tim Cook as a potential CEO candidate.It didn’t take long for Trump to begin softening his approach, making it clear he’d welcome Huang back into the role of CEO even if Nvidia’s own board wasn’t ready to do so. Behind the scenes, the Trump administration was working to grease the landing for Huang’s return. And soon, Nvidia’s board changed its tune: Barely a week after insisting they all agreed to shut the door on Huang’s return, they voted unanimously to reinstate him as CEO, president, and board director.“There’s nothing wrong with a comeback,” Trump said in a celebratory call to CNBC.Trump then posted an image on Truth Social of Huang transposed onto Trump’s own body in the infamous photo of him raising his fist after being shot at a campaign rally. In his raised fist, Huang-on-Trump’s-body is clutching a scarlet bra, holding it high in the air.“There’s nothing wrong with a comeback”Even after a decisive blow to the president’s power as Democrats swept the midterm elections, Trump appears to maintain his position as a corporate kingmaker. Trump said he spoke with Huang the night prior to his reinstatement and had been in communication with the board both “directly and indirectly.” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement that “President Trump was totally involved” in the board’s decision — Trump decided near the end of last week that he wanted to lead efforts to get Huang reappointed, per The New York Times, so he asked Vice President JD Vance to act as a liaison between Huang and Nvidia’s board, providing reassurances that the move wouldn’t pose a security risk.
